name: Anti-5G necklace

card.summary: A negative-ion pendant sold as protection from 5G radiation and for wellness; it is worn as a necklace.
card.note: Some such products measured as radioactive; the Netherlands banned them in 2021.

quick.overview:
Anti-5G necklaces are pendants and jewellery sold as releasing negative ions and shielding the wearer from 5G radiation, with wellness claims attached. Buyers wear them as an accessory with a perceived health payoff.

In December 2021 the Dutch regulator ANVS issued a product alert saying several such items, including pendants and bracelets, emit ionising radiation.
quick.how: The pendant is worn on a cord or chain around the neck, usually continuously. They are sold online as quantum, scalar or negative-ion jewellery.
quick.risks: The ANVS said the items emit ionising radiation at low levels and that long wear could damage tissue and DNA. A 2021 study reported yearly doses up to 1.22 millisieverts, above the 1 mSv limit recommended by ICRP. The Netherlands prohibited their sale and asked owners to store them safely and contact the authority.

lead: Anti-5G necklaces belong to the family of negative ion products, jewellery marketed as releasing negative ions with wellness benefits and often as protection against 5G radiation. These claims lack scientific support and sales are linked to 5G conspiracy theories.[1]

In December 2021 the Dutch nuclear regulator ANVS warned that about ten products, including a Quantum Pendant, several Magnetix bracelets and necklaces, an Energy Armor necklace and a sleep mask, emit ionising radiation. Sellers were told to stop and owners to store the items safely.[2]

angle.text: Wearers use the pendant as a wellness accessory. Any appearance link is indirect and rests on general wellbeing claims.

infobox: Up to 1.22 mSv/year in a 2021 study

paras: Many negative ion products contain radioactive substances. A 2021 study in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health found yearly doses up to 1.22 millisieverts, above the 1 mSv limit recommended by the ICRP.[1]
Coverage reported that the products remained on sale online after the Dutch ban.[1][2]
No studies found on health benefits of these pendants.

timeline.event: Dutch ANVS issues a product alert and prohibits sale.[2]
